source: Zhang, Wang, Chen (2025/2026) Scientific judgment drifts over time in AI ideation (arXiv 2511.04964)
finding: This study builds its idea generator on the Uzzi mix: each prompt pairs a 'conventional' idea (the scientist's own latest paper) with a 'novel' idea (a highly cited paper), either from another department (cross-domain) or the same one (in-domain). The text I read does not report a cross-domain versus in-domain rating contrast, so the mix is used but not tested against all-distant or all-conventional sets. It also shows that expert ratings of the same idea drift.
numbers: 63 researchers, 6 departments, 7,938 ratings, two waves. 50 cross-domain + 50 in-domain pairs per person; top 3 of each kept. Test-retest ICC of overall quality 0.59-0.74; originality 0.60 [0.40,0.77]. Human-written control idea beat AI ideas on overall quality in both waves.
quote: we did not assume all ideas generated with this method will be of high quality
limits: Single institution. Ratings are the only outcome (no executable check). Gap 1 is not closed by this paper.
agent_relevance: Shows the mix is a workable generator design (one conventional anchor plus one distant seed, over-generate, then select). Also warns that any originality rater is noisy: ICC about 0.6 for originality, so use a verifier for selection.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) The Ramon Llull's Thinking Machine for Automated Ideation (COLM 2025 workshop, arXiv 2508.19200)
finding: Combining LLM prompts from the most trending elements (Top) versus randomly sampled elements (Random) shows the distance trade-off directly: random, more distant combinations double lexical diversity but are far less relevant to the field. The authors say diversity and coverage do not imply novelty or utility.
numbers: 100 ideas per arm. Diversity (distinct-1): Top 0.21, Random 0.41, Si 2024 human-filtered 0.29, Yu 2024 0.29. Relevance to ACL 2025 titles: Top 0.11, Random 0.05, Si 0.28, Yu 0.18. Similarity: Top 0.26, Random 0.23.
limits: Title-level lexical metrics only. No correctness, no execution, no expert novelty rating. Random is not a controlled distance.
agent_relevance: A forced-distance seed buys diversity and loses relevance. A conventional core is the natural fix, but this paper did not test it. Gap 1 stays open; gap 8 gets 'diversity rises, relevance falls'.

source: Ustyuzhanin, Trofimova, Zuenko (2026) Citations Are Late (arXiv 2610.07397)
finding: An independent group tests displacement of an incumbent directly. A content signal built on whether abstracts adopt, contest or stress limits of the incumbent paradigm detects the RNN-to-Transformer shift years before the citation-based disruption index (CD5) can. This ties displacement to a paper's stance toward a named incumbent, and shows the citation index is structurally late.
numbers: Content signal crosses a pre-registered threshold in 2016-Q1; CD5 monitor cannot observe the 2017 breakthrough until 2022-Q2 (5-year window): lead of 25 quarters. Versus the breakthrough date the lead is 5 quarters in NLP and contemporaneous in vision (14-19 quarter lead over CD5 in vision). Paradigm-reliance label kappa 0.83 on human-recoverable items; keyword-blind AUC 0.9 reproduced on human labels.
limits: Two shifts (NLP, vision), both ML. Not a test of functional equivalence or of recombination. LLM-extracted labels. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 4: the trigger for displacement is a named incumbent that candidates contest. The schema step 'state the incumbent answer and what job it does' is the same variable. It also confirms that the payoff of displacement is only visible late (gap 9).

source: Lu, Wang, Li, Jiang, Khudanpur, Jiang, Khashabi (2025) Benchmarking Language Model Creativity: A Case Study on Code Generation (NAACL 2025, arXiv 2407.09007)
finding: On Codeforces problems with unit-test verification, forcing GPT-4 to avoid techniques used in earlier solutions (Denial Prompting) raises divergent creativity but destroys correctness. Reasoning strategies (MCTS, self-correction, planning, sampling) do not improve both at once. This is the only executable-verifier test of forced novelty versus correctness I found.
numbers: 199 problems, 30 human solutions each. GPT-4 by constraint state t=0..5: pass@1 16.1, 11.6, 7.1, 5.2, 2.3, 2.1 (%); constraint following 100 down to 14.4; divergent creative 4.5 up to 15.3; convergent creative 16.2 down to 0.0; NeoGauge 1.0, 1.4, 0.9, 0.5, 0, 0. Humans have greater convergent creativity than LLMs before state 3. Only MCTS lifts divergent creativity; none lifts NeoGauge much (k=5 samples; CodeGemma-7B for MCTS, GPT-3.5 for the others).
limits: Novelty is defined as using techniques absent from human solutions, a narrow definition. GPT-4 era models. Competitive programming only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3, partly answered: the novelty edge does not survive when execution is checked. The more the agent is pushed away from the known method, the faster correctness falls. A distance budget with a verifier gate is needed.

source: Ye, Gu, Zhao, Yin, Wang (2024) Assessing the Creativity of LLMs in Proposing Novel Solutions to Mathematical Problems (CreativeMath, arXiv 2410.18336)
finding: Given k known solutions to a competition math problem, LLMs propose a new one. Gemini-1.5-Pro gets most correct solutions that are also novel. More reference solutions raise correctness but lower novelty. On harder problems accuracy drops but the share of novel correct answers rises. Correctness and novelty are judged by LLM evaluators.
numbers: Gemini-1.5-Pro: correctness 69.92%, novelty ratio 66.94%, novelty-to-correctness 95.75%. 100% correctness at k=4. Across difficulty (k=1): correctness 71.80% on AMC 8 down to about 35% on USAMO/IMO; novelty-to-correctness 55.39% up to 83.01%.
limits: Novelty and correctness both LLM-judged (GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro as evaluators), no formal proof check.
agent_relevance: Math: novelty among correct answers is not scarce, correctness is. Showing prior solutions lowers novelty, so a 'name the incumbent first' step costs diversity (gap 4) and must be offset by an explicit 'differ from this' instruction.

source: Zhang, Diddee, Holm, Liu, Liu, Samuel, Wang, Ippolito (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Human-like Diversity (COLM 2025, arXiv 2504.05228)
finding: Frontier models give fewer than 3 meaningfully distinct answers in 10 samples at temperature 1. Larger models in a family are less diverse than smaller ones. Telling the model to be creative barely helps. Showing the model its earlier answers and asking for a different one (in-context regeneration) restores roughly human-level diversity with no loss of utility.
numbers: 1,100 prompts (100 curated + 1,000 WildChat), 20 models, distinct_k and a quality-weighted utility score. Closed models Claude 3, Gemini, GPT-4o score below 4 of 10 on cumulative utility. 8 author-written human baselines. With in-context regeneration GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceed human cumulative utility; paraphrasing and a 'be unique' system prompt are only marginal.
limits: Prompts are everyday open questions, not verifiable tasks. Distinctness judged by a trained classifier. Does not test a seed that is forced to be semantically far.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, partly answered: the cheapest forced-distance move is conditioning on prior candidates and demanding a different one. Quality did not fall here, but correctness was not checked.

source: Jiang, Chai, Li, Liu, Fok, Dziri, Tsvetkov, Sap, Albalak, Choi (2025/2026) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (arXiv 2510.22954)
finding: Across many models, open-ended answers collapse onto a few clusters. Each model repeats itself, and different models repeat each other. Raising sampling temperature or using min-p does not fix it.
numbers: Infinity-Chat: 26K real queries, 31,250 human annotations (25 raters per item), 70+ models studied. 'Time metaphor' query: 25 models x 50 responses collapse into two clusters. Same-model pairwise embedding similarity exceeds 0.8 in 79% of cases at top-p 0.9, T=1.0; across models 71-82% similarity (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82, vs GPT-4o 0.81). Even min-p with T=2.0 stays above 0.8 on average. Within-prompt similarity averaged 0.821 over 42 models.
limits: Similarity from one embedding model (text-embedding-3-small). Open-ended chat queries, not verifiable tasks. Does not test forced-distance seeds.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model or from many models are much less independent than they look, so equal-token sampling gives few independent candidates. Supports forcing distance in the prompt rather than relying on temperature.

source: Zhang, Yu, Chong, Sicilia, Tomz, Manning, Shi (2026) Verbalized Sampling (arXiv 2510.01171 v4)
finding: Asking the model to list several answers with their probabilities raises diversity without hurting factual accuracy or safety, and the diverse synthetic math questions it produces train better student models. The authors trace mode collapse to annotators preferring typical text.
numbers: Creative writing: diversity 1.6-2.1x over direct prompting. Synthetic math (1,000 questions per method; GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash generators; SFT on Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-1.7B and 4B; MATH500, OlympiadBench, Minerva): average accuracy 32.8 baseline, 30.6 direct, 33.7 sequence, 34.3 multi-turn, 36.1 VS-Standard, 37.5 VS-CoT. More capable models benefit more.
limits: Gain is on a downstream pipeline (data for fine-tuning), not on the same model's own answer correctness. Diversity is of the kind 'many answers per call', not distance-controlled.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: diversity can be raised at no accuracy cost when it feeds a verifier-checked pipeline. Evidence for a 'verbalize k candidates with weights, then verify' step as an alternative to a forced-distance seed.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and Innovation in Scientists' Research Strategies (ASR; arXiv 1302.6906)
finding: Re-read this session. Risky strategies (new relationships, jumps) pay more citations on average but not enough to cover the extra failure risk, so the conservative repeat strategy maximizes expected citations. The break-even numbers are confirmed.
numbers: Repeat statements 85.8% of the literature versus 14.2% for new and jump; jumps 1.8%. Mean citations 1983-2002: repeat 8.38, new 11.00, jump 12.90. Indifference needs p(new)=0.76 p(repeat) and p(jump)=0.65 p(repeat). Strategy surprisal explains 29.2% of mean citation variation and 28.6% of the SD (a tenfold rarer strategy: +2.26 citations).
limits: Biomedical chemistry (chemical relations in MEDLINE) only; citations as payoff; unpublished failures are invisible.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no LLM equivalent found. The human numbers give a prior for budget: about 1 in 7 moves new or jump, and jumps need to succeed at least 65% as often as repeats to break even. For the agent, estimate that ratio with a verifier on a calibration set.

source: Liu, Dubova, Conklin, Harada, Griffiths (2026) Assessing the effect of cross-domain mapping on creativity in humans and LLMs (arXiv 2603.19087) - second reading
finding: Second reading adds the rater and trade-off details behind the distance threshold. Originality trades off hard against feasibility, so the distance gain is measured on the very dimension that rises when the source is far, while feasibility falls. For o3 and Claude-Sonnet-4 the benefit appears in the farther half of pairings.
numbers: Originality vs feasibility rho = -0.74 (p<.001); originality vs utility -0.08; investment-worthiness driven by utility (0.71) not originality (0.23). Split-half reliability: originality .81, feasibility .80, utility .73. o3 and Claude-Sonnet-4: all pairs beta=0.02 (p=.64); top 50% most distant 0.12 (p=.029); top 10% 0.24 (p=.024). Pooled LLMs: cross-domain below the user-need prompt for close pairs; gap gone once the closest 20% were dropped. Human top-10% ideas under cross-domain mapping were less useful (utility gap 0.81, p<.001).
limits: Product design with lay raters, one embedding distance (Wikipedia-based), 7 LLMs, two strong ones carry the threshold result. No execution check.
agent_relevance: Gap 2, partly answered: the source must be far; the threshold depends on model strength (strong models: farther half; weaker models: need the closest fifth removed). The rater measures originality, not correctness, so this is not a correct-answer threshold.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New Directions in Science Emerge from Disconnection and Discord (J. Informetrics; arXiv 2103.03398) - definitions
finding: The positive atypicality-disruption link is shown for a thin tail, defined from Uzzi z-scores (10th percentile of the paper's journal-pair z-scores; lower is more atypical). Only a small share of papers qualify. The link is stronger in computer science and engineering, weaker in biology, chemistry and physics.
numbers: Microsoft Academic Graph: 87,860,684 articles; 35,431,832 with citations and references. Highly atypical papers 2.3% of the sample, 3.9% in 1970 down to 1.4% in 2000. Highly atypical papers disrupt 61% of the time vs 36% for conventional. 1970 cohort 87,475 papers. Uzzi's mix (atypical + typical) still best predicts being highly cited. KS tests D=0.14 (z-median, disruptive vs developing), 0.09 (z-min). Disruption takes about ten years to converge.
limits: MAG, journals as the unit, outcome is the share of papers labelled disruptive, not mean D. Cohort analysis by decade.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the 61 vs 36 result is about the extreme tail and a share-based outcome. It differs from Li 2025 on every definition, see d12.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas? (arXiv 2506.15959) - definitions
finding: Overlapping authors to Lin 2022 report the opposite sign: high A-index papers have lower mean D in every discipline, period and team-size stratum. Differences from Lin 2022: OpenAlex not MAG; 1965-2020 all papers not a decade cohort; an A-index scale with top 5% at A>22.9 (higher means more atypical, the reverse of z); outcome is mean D within A bins, not the share disruptive. The text I read does not discuss or reconcile the earlier 61% vs 36% result.
numbers: 40,935,251 articles (1965-2020) in the correlation figure, 40,453,825 in the time-trend figure. Top 5% displacing papers D>0.04. Frames the result as: atypicality extends concepts into new topics, disruption replaces a dominant idea within its topic.
limits: Preprint. No matched-definition rerun on either dataset. No test of the tail alone.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: no direct reconciliation exists. Plausible reading: a tail effect (Lin) versus a bulk slope (Li), which would make atypicality a weak positive signal only for the extreme tail. Untested; do not use A as a selection signal without a verifier.

source: Huang (2026) Catalyst Papers in AI Research: A Landscape on ICLR 2017-2025 (arXiv 2607.05401)
finding: An independent author separates cross-topic bridges (recombination) from within-topic redirectors (displacement) with embedding clusters, not the Li et al. method. Both types are small and overlap little with each other; review scores say nothing about later disruptiveness.
numbers: 36,113 ICLR papers; 113 HDBSCAN topic clusters on UMAP of 1,024-d OpenAI embeddings (66.5% of papers covered). Topic initiators 8.5%, topic bridges 9.8%, within-topic redirectors 7.1%, recognition-misaligned 3.1%; union 22.2%. 26.4% of initiators are also redirectors; 36.6% of misaligned also bridges. Topic bridges precede 11.52x cross-topic citation flow; initiators 7.55x topic-share growth. Embedding disruptiveness measure AUC 0.83 for highly cited papers vs 0.60 CD, 0.49 node2vec, 0.42 LLM rater. Reviewer score vs disruptiveness rho about 0.005; accepted and rejected papers have the same mean EDM (p=0.11).
limits: One venue, AI only. Taxonomy defined by the author. Does not test whether bridges are less disruptive than redirectors.
agent_relevance: Gap 10, partial: a different topic model supports bridging and replacing being separate paths. Gap 4: LLM raters and reviewer scores are poor selection signals for later impact; use verifier outcomes.

source: Radensky, Shahid, Fok, Siangliulue, Hope, Weld (2026) Scideator: Human-LLM Compound System for Scientific Ideation (CAIS 2026; arXiv 2409.14634)
finding: A novelty checker that retrieves prior work and compares it facet by facet finds known overlap far better than keyword or embedding retrieval alone. An embedding filter without the LLM facet re-ranker surfaces the known overlapping paper in the top 10 only about one time in ten. Scideator also combines facets from near, far and very-far papers on purpose.
numbers: Retrieval ablation on 58 ideas with known overlap (13 not-novel + 45 published NLP papers): complete system 89.66%; relevance re-ranker instead of facet re-ranker 13.79%; embedding filtering only 10.34%; snippet only 8.62%; keyword only 5.17%. Classifier (26 novel, 17 not novel): zero-shot accuracy 0.68 / F1 0.65; AI Scientist prompt 0.47 / 0.44; OpenReview examples 0.59 / 0.43; expert in-context 0.78 / 0.77; with reasoning 0.81 / 0.79. Participants (17 completed the novelty task) used far facets less, mostly because of lower perceived relevance.
limits: Retrieval is Semantic Scholar plus LLM re-ranking, not a cheap non-LLM gate. NLP papers only. Novel ideas have no ground truth for the retrieval test.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a cheap embedding-distance gate alone is not enough to detect disguised overlap; facet-level comparison (purpose and mechanism) plus retrieval is what worked. Run the novelty gate on purpose-mechanism pairs, not whole text.

source: Chan and Schunn (2015); Chan, Dow, Schunn (near vs far design studies); Fu et al. (2013) - from search-result snippets only
finding: Search-result snippets only (the links returned 404 when fetched). Human design studies reported that moderate distance is best (Fu et al. 2013, inverted U), that conceptually closer sources helped more in a web-platform study, and that the benefit of far combinations depends on how much the design has converged when the combination is made. Some work argues far analogies have no clear general advantage or cause fixation.
numbers: No exact numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened. Treat as pointers to follow, not as evidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 9: the human literature already hints at an inverted U and a timing effect, so the agent should treat distance and timing as tunable variables, not assume monotone gains.

source: Pezeshkpour and Hruschka (2026) AutoPyVerifier: Learning Compact Executable Verifiers for LLM Outputs (arXiv 2604.22937, abstract page)
finding: An LLM can propose Python verifier functions that are searched into a compact set matching a target objective. Executable verifiers are more reliable than LLM judges but narrower.
numbers: Up to 55.0 F1 points over the initial LLM-written verifier sets across math, coding, function calling and instruction following. Giving the discovered verifiers to an LLM as a tool raised downstream accuracy by up to 17.0 points.
limits: Abstract page only. Verifies correctness, not novelty. Tested on existing benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: supports the scoring design (mix vs all-distant vs all-conventional, equal tokens, executable verifier). It does not test the mix. Cheap executable checks can serve as the common yardstick.

source: Gap-search negative result (this session): no study found for gaps 1, 5, 7, 10 as posed
finding: No LLM study found that compares a conventional-core-plus-distant-add-on set against all-distant and all-conventional sets (gap 1), that measures an LLM budget share for distant moves (gap 7), that tests a non-LLM novelty gate on disguised copying (gap 5), or that replicates functional equivalence outside the Wu/Evans group (gap 10, only a partial hit in d13). The web search quota was exhausted early, and the arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned 429. Sources came from direct arXiv PDF fetches and earlier downloads.
limits: Search coverage was thin. It is 'not found with limited search', not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Treat gaps 1, 5, 7 and 10 as open and run them as our own experiments.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) read with Ustyuzhanin et al. (2026) on delayed payoff (Wang 2017 is a05)
finding: Delayed payoff is documented three ways: slow start and later more top-1% hits for highly novel papers (Wang 2017, recorded as a05), disruption scores that need ten years or longer to converge (Lin 2022, read this session), and a five-year citation window that cannot see a 2017 breakthrough until 2022 (Ustyuzhanin 2026). All are citation-based; none tests LLM candidates with an extra revision round.
numbers: Lin 2022: ten years or longer to converge; the DNA paper D rises from 0.2 (1953) to nearly 0.8 ten years later and 0.96 by 2018. CD5 lag: 2022-Q2 for a 2017 event.
limits: Human citation time scales, not model refinement rounds. No intervention.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no LLM evidence. One extra revision round for distant candidates before ranking is a cheap test of whether early weakness is repairable by revision.
